passage: On the first day of term at the Tumkur government high school, the headmaster pinned a red 'Discipline Prefect' badge on Harsha's shirt. Harsha was fifteen and soft-spoken, so at home in the mirror he practised a frown and a short, hard 'Line up!' It felt like a costume. By the second week, the frown came without practice. He began stopping juniors at the gate for untucked shirts and making them stand by the flagpole. On Thursday he took Gargi's tiffin because she ate a chapati in the corridor, and when she protested he said, 'Rules,' and felt nothing much. Walking home, his little brother asked why he talked like a policeman now. Harsha opened his mouth to deny it, then realised he couldn't remember when it had stopped feeling like acting.

qa.q: What did Harsha practise in the mirror at home?
qa.a: Harsha practised a frown and a short, hard 'Line up!'

qa.q: What does Harsha feeling 'nothing much' when taking Gargi's tiffin suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the tough role now feels normal, so Harsha has gone numb to something he once would have found unkind.

qa.q: What turning point could help Harsha step back from the role?
qa.a: His brother's question about talking like a policeman; Harsha could use it to return the tiffin and decide which rules really need a hard tone.

qa.q: How might Gargi see the new prefect?
qa.a: Gargi probably sees Harsha as harsh and unfair, taking her food over one chapati and brushing off her protest with 'Rules'.

grounding: Shows a soft-spoken teenager whose practised prefect toughness becomes natural and shifts what he thinks is acceptable.

passage: The red armband was too big, so Soo-ah pinned it tighter. Exam-week hall monitor at her Seoul high school meant standing at the stairwell and stopping anyone who ran. On Monday she said, 'Please walk,' and felt silly. By Wednesday she had learned that a flat voice worked better, and that people stepped aside for the armband. By Friday she was writing names in the notebook for talking, for laughing, for a dropped pencil case. When Leila, her friend from art club, skidded around the corner, Soo-ah didn't smile. 'Name.' 'Soo-ah, it's me.' 'Name, please.' Leila spelled out her name slowly, staring at Soo-ah. Only on the bus did Soo-ah replay it and feel a strange cold drop in her stomach. It had felt so normal at the time.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah writing names in the notebook for by Friday?
qa.a: For talking, for laughing, for a dropped pencil case.

qa.q: What does the cold drop in Soo-ah's stomach on the bus suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Soo-ah feels uneasy, even a little ashamed, realising late that the armband's toughness had taken over and she had treated a friend like a stranger 😔

qa.q: What could Soo-ah do on Monday to step back out of the role?
qa.a: Soo-ah could apologise to Leila and decide to stop only runners, the rule she was actually given.

qa.q: What is it like for Leila when her friend demands her name?
qa.a: Leila feels hurt and shut out, spelling her name slowly and staring, as if she doesn't recognise Soo-ah.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager whose hall-monitor armband slowly makes harshness feel natural, even toward a friend.

passage: At Sunrise Residential School, the mess prefect got a whistle and a clipboard. Yogesh, sixteen, had laughed at the last one for strutting. In his first week he blew the whistle only for grace. In the second, he started making the Class 7 table wait until every plate was stacked perfectly. By the fourth week he had a rule nobody had given him: juniors who spilled dal had to hold their plate up while the others ate. Dhruv, twelve, stood with his thin arms trembling, dal dripping onto the floor. Yogesh watched the clock without blinking. That night his roommate said, 'You're worse than the old prefect.' Yogesh started to argue, then stopped. It had felt fair. That was what unsettled him.

qa.q: What rule did Yogesh create by the fourth week?
qa.a: Juniors who spilled dal had to hold their plate up while the others ate.

qa.q: Why does Yogesh feel unsettled after his roommate's comment?
qa.a: Yogesh realises the punishment had felt fair to him, which shows how far the role has shifted what he accepts.

qa.q: What choice could Yogesh make at breakfast the next morning?
qa.a: Yogesh could drop the plate-holding rule, apologise to Dhruv, and ask the housemaster which rules the mess prefect is really meant to enforce.

qa.q: What is it like for Dhruv, holding his plate up?
qa.a: Dhruv, twelve, is shamed in front of everyone and struggling, his thin arms trembling while the others eat.

grounding: Shows a teenage mess prefect who once mocked strutting gradually inventing harsh rules until they feel fair.

passage:
Dear Ishita,

You asked what being bus prefect is like. I'll be honest, since you're my cousin and won't tell anyone. The little ones call me Prefect Didi.

In June the principal gave me a badge and a list of rules. I didn't know how to be strict, so I copied last year's prefect: arms folded, loud voice, "Sit down NOW." It felt like wearing someone else's jacket.

But it's November now and the jacket fits. Yesterday a Class 5 boy was singing, and I made him stand for the whole ride home. He's nine. I didn't even think about it. It was only when his little sister started crying at his stop that I heard myself, like a recording.

In June I would never have done that. Now it feels normal, and that's what scares me. I don't think I'm a mean person. I think I've been playing one so long I forgot.

Write back soon,
Aditi

qa.q: How long did Aditi make the Class 5 boy stand?
qa.a: She made him stand for the whole ride home.

qa.q: What scares Aditi when she thinks about the bus ride?
qa.a: She is scared that being harsh now feels normal, as if she has been playing a mean prefect so long she forgot it was an act.

qa.q: What turning point made Aditi notice the change, and what could she do next?
qa.a: The boy's little sister crying at his stop made her hear herself; she could apologise to the boy and drop the copied voice to find her own way of keeping order.

qa.q: How might the nine-year-old boy see Aditi now?
qa.a: He might see her as frightening and unfair, since he was punished for singing and had to stand in front of everyone the whole ride.

grounding: A teenage bus prefect who began by copying a tough manner finds the harshness has come to feel natural and changes what she thinks is acceptable.

passage: "Siddharth, you want to know why the juniors were scared of me last term? Okay. I got the role of the jail warden in our school play. Big boots, a fake moustache, a baton. Our drama teacher told us, 'Stay in character, even off stage, it helps.' So I did. At rehearsals I marched around and barked at the Class 8 kids who played prisoners. Everyone laughed; it was part of the fun. But after about three weeks I noticed I was barking at them in the canteen too, with no boots on. I made one of them give up his seat for me, and it felt completely normal. My mother said, 'Manoj, beta, why do you keep saying Silence at dinner?' After the final show I took off the moustache and still sounded like him. It took me a month to stop."

qa.q: What props came with the role of the jail warden?
qa.a: Big boots, a fake moustache and a baton.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel when he made the junior give up his seat in the canteen?
qa.a: It felt completely normal to him, which shows the role had started to change what he thought was acceptable.

qa.q: What could the drama teacher have done differently?
qa.a: The teacher could have set a clear line that the character stays on stage, and checked in on how the junior actors were being treated off stage.

qa.q: How might the Class 8 juniors have experienced Manoj off stage?
qa.a: They probably felt scared and confused, since the barking no longer felt like a game once it followed them into the canteen.

grounding: A teenager cast as a harsh warden stays in character until the toughness spills into real life and starts to feel natural.
